extracted.intended_audience: NLP / machine-learning researchers and practitioners working on sarcasm detection, fake-news detection, and dataset curation
extracted.subtask_description: Creation and release of a labeled news-headlines dataset for sarcasm detection (sarcastic headlines from TheOnion vs. real headlines from HuffPost), including curation method, record schema, statistics, and example code for reading the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source selection (TheOnion for sarcastic, HuffPost for non-sarcastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collected headlines from two news websites: TheOnion aims at producing sarcastic versions of current events, whereas HuffPost publishes real news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For TheOnion, collect from 'News in Brief' and 'News in Photos' categories (which are sarcastic). For HuffPost, use archive links and extract headlines. Choosing professional news sites yields more formal language and higher-quality labels than hashtag-supervised Twitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label quality (high-quality labels from TheOnion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the sole purpose of TheOnion is to publish sarcastic news, we get high-quality labels with much less noise as compared to Twitter datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer sources where sarcasm/satire is produced intentionally to avoid noisy supervision methods like hashtag-based labels on social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained text requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike tweets which are replies to other tweets, the news headlines we obtained are self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-contained headlines reduce the need for external conversational context and make it easier for models to learn sarcastic cues from the headline text alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal language / low informal-noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Since news headlines are written by professionals in a formal manner, there are no spelling mistakes and informal usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal language reduces vocabulary sparsity, increases chances of finding pre-trained embeddings, and avoids issues common in Twitter data such as misspellings and abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record schema / annotation fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Each record in the dataset consists of three attributes: is_sarcastic: 1 if the record is sarcastic otherwise 0; headline: the headline of the news article; article_link: link to the original news article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this simple binary annotation schema and include the article link so additional context/text can be extracted if needed by downstream tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include source links to enable further data extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: We include an article link corresponding to each headline so that more text regarding the news can be extracted as needed by any Machine Learning task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing article links allows researchers to augment headline-level data with article body, metadata, or context when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class balancing via downsampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Since Huffington has significantly more news headlines, we downsample the data to approximately match the number of sarcastic headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining sources with different base volumes, downsample the larger source to reduce class imbalance before shuffling and combining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shuffling and vertical integration
rubrics_metrics.description: We then do vertical integration of data and shuffle all the records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After merging sources and balancing, shuffle records to avoid ordering artifacts and to mix classes for training/validation splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: No additional preprocessing necessary for high-quality headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the headline text comes from professional news websites and has reasonably good quality (no misspellings, abbreviations, etc.), we did not do any additional pre-processing on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If source text is already formal and clean, minimal preprocessing may be acceptable; nevertheless, document any preprocessing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curation tools and crawling method
rubrics_metrics.description: We make use of open-source tools like BeautifulSoup, Selenium, and Chrome Driver to curate the dataset. For collecting data from TheOnion, we use News in Brief and News in Photos as the base link. Extract link and headline text using BeautifulSoup. Simulate button click with Selenium to go to the next page and repeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use programmatic scraping with page navigation simulation where necessary; document base links/categories, extraction selectors, and navigation strategy so the crawl is reproducible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset size and class counts (statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset contains about 28K headlines out of which 13K are sarcastic (28,619 records; 13,635 sarcastic; 14,984 non-sarcastic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit counts for total records and per-class counts so users can assess scale and suitability for deep-learning methods versus small manual-labeled datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-trained embedding coverage statistic
rubrics_metrics.description: % of pre-trained word embeddings not available — for Headlines dataset 23.35% (compared to Semeval dataset 35.53%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report fraction of words missing from common pre-trained embeddings (e.g., word2vec) to indicate vocabulary coverage and potential need for custom embeddings or handling out-of-vocabulary tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation against Twitter/hashtag supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter datasets collected using hashtag-based supervision have noisy labels; people use very informal language on Twitter which introduces sparsity in vocabulary; many tweets are replies and require contextual tweets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing datasets for sarcasm detection, consider whether label acquisition (hashtags vs. manual vs. source-driven) and the medium's language style will introduce noise or necessitate extra context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data access and example read code
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a code snippet to read the dataset: JSON lines parsing example (parse_data yields json.loads(l)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply example I/O code (here Python snippet) so users can quickly load the dataset; indicate file format (newline-delimited JSON) explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential use cases documented
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset can be used for Sarcasm Detection, fake news detection, and to study humor and irony-related linguistic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List plausible downstream tasks and provide pointers to example implementations (linked PyTorch implementation) to help users get started.
